Introduction
In many applications of statistical learning, the observations collected to train a supervised
model are not sampled using an i.i.d. mechanism. Instead, the observations adhere to some
correlation structure due to the nature of the data collection. The correlation between observations can arise from spatiotemporal relationships within the samples, as is common in
neuroscience and ecology Roberts et al. [2017]. It can also capture clustering of observations into groups, as is common, for example, in electronic medical records (same hospital,
same city) and in computer vision (images of the same person). Within predictive modeling contexts, the presence of such correlation structures can influence model construction
methodologies, resulting in a diverse array of approaches that span both traditional and
modern techniques.
A simple example for this kind of violation of the i.i.d. sampling is when multiply
samples are collected from each object, resulting in a correlation between them. A standard
modeling method to address this kind of correlation structure is linear mixed models (LMM,
Verbeke et al. [1997]) with random intercept for grouped data:

effect covariates, β ∈Rp is the fixed coefficients vector, δi is the random intercept of object
i, the ϵ’s are the iid errors, and y is the observed outcome. In this setting, observations
yi,j1 and yi,j2 are correlated because they share the same realization of δi. This kind of
statistical model is named a mixed model, because it is an integration of the fixed effect,
which is characterized by the fixed vector β, and the random effect, specified by the random
vector δ.
Some other modeling methods are discussed in the traditional literature for dealing
with correlated data, such as Gaussian process regression (GPR, Williams and Rasmussen
[1995]), generalized least squares (GLS, Hansen [2007], and generalized linear mixed models
(GLMM, Stroup [2012] ). These methods have been shown to be practical in various fields

(Jiang and Nguyen [2007]), such as medicine (Brown and Prescott [2014]), geo-statistics
Goovaerts [1999], genetic (Maddison [1990]), and ecology (Roberts et al. [2017]). In recent years, some studies [Simchoni and Rosset, 2021, Tran et al., 2020, Xiong et al., 2019]
suggested combining the idea of random effects with Deed Neural Networks (DNN), and
showed promising results. These approaches involve advanced methods to solve the optimization problem that takes into account the correlation structure, while maintaining the
fitting procedure feasible in terms of computational resources. With any of the methods
described above, one can be interested in using the fitted model to predict a future outcome
of the dependent variable.
Given a statistical-based prediction task, it is of interest to evaluate the prediction
error of the model in use. Usually, the model selection and tuning procedures are based on
prediction error estimation, thus, it is important to obtain a reliable estimate. A widely
used prediction error measure is the K-fold cross-validation (CV), ([Stone, 1974, Hastie
et al., 2009]), which is also the focus of this study. However, as discussed in the literature
[Roberts et al., 2017, Anderson et al., 2019], CV estimation might be biased and not suitable
when the assumption of i.i.d. sampling is violated. Intuitively, if the correlation structure
among training data differs from that between training data and prediction points, regular
CV may inaccurately assess the generalization error, which is the expected loss of a learning.
Traditionally, efforts to address this challenge of CV when dealing with changing correlation
structures have focused on designing sampling approaches that would allow cross validation
to give valid scores for model evaluation and selection, exactly or approximately, such as the
leave cluster out (LCO) approach Rice and Silverman [1991], or leave observation from each
cluster out (LOFCO,Wu and Zhang [2002]). However, these methods are only applicable to
particular correlation structures and necessitate a balanced data design, where the number
of folds is dictated by the data structure.
The paper Rabinowicz and Rosset [2022a] introduces a new perspective on the CV estimation in the presence of correlated data, mainly in the context of linear models with
squared error loss. One major contribution of that paper was to precisely identify the condi3

tions for the unbiasedness of the CV estimator, concluding that it can also be unbiased if the
correlated structure is preserved in the prediction points. In addition, the paper presents
a bias-corrected CV measure, denoted CVc, that was shown to be suitable in various scenarios where CV is biased due to the correlations in the data. In this study, we extend the
results and the methodology of Rabinowicz and Rosset [2022a] to correct the CV estimator
from linear models with square loss, to general models and general prediction criteria. In
particular, we provide a framework for evaluating and selecting models for classification
tasks in the presence of correlation structures. We derive a surprisingly general expression
for the bias of CV for a class of prediction quality scores, independent of the model in
use, and demonstrate that it can serve to explicitly describe this bias when using the most
common measures of classification prediction error: 0-1 loss, cross entropy (Bernoulli loglikelihood) and hinge loss. The expressions we derive are simple and completely general,
in that they do not depend on the true model or the modeling approach used for building
the models. However, quantifying these general expressions in any specific setting requires
knowledge of the model form and/or the model parameters. One approach we present for
estimating this bias in practice is based on parametric bootstrap and is widely applicable;
however, it can be computationally prohibitive in realistic settings. Therefore, we also
propose several efficient approximations that apply to specific model settings, in particular
when the true model is a GLMM. We also demonstrate that these methods can be used
to approximately estimate the bias of the CV estimator in modern deep learning models
and to better evaluate the prediction error. This paper is an expanded version of the published conference paper Yuval and Rosset [2025]. The corresponding code is available at
https://github.com/OrenYuv/CVc-for-General-Models.

standard cross-validation may not be suitable for these settings.
1.2
The challenge of estimating the CV bias and correcting it
The main challenge is to identify the conditions under which the CV estimator is unbiased
and when it is not. We then derive a general expression for the bias of CV, which can be
applied to a variety of models and prediction criteria. The expression for the bias depends on
the model's true parameters, the model's form, and the prediction loss. The challenge is to
express this bias in a way that can be practically estimated, given that the true model parameters
are unknown and that the model form is either known or can be estimated from the data.
We proceed in two steps. First, we derive a general expression for the bias of CV. Second, we
find an estimate for this bias, based on parametric bootstrap or other approximations. Once
the bias is estimated, we can adjust the CV estimator by adding this bias to it, thereby creating
a bias-corrected CV estimator, which is expected to have lower bias and hopefully better
performances in terms of prediction error estimation.
1.3
The paper's contributions
The paper's contributions can be broken down into the following parts:

1. A general framework for evaluating and selecting models for classification tasks in the presence of correlation structures.
2. Derivation of a general expression for the bias of the CV estimator for a class of prediction quality scores, which is independent of the model in use.
3. Simple and general expressions for the bias in the case of 0-1 loss, cross entropy loss, and hinge loss.
4. A parametric bootstrap approach for estimating the bias in practice, which is computationally applicable.
5. Efficient approximations for specific model settings, such as generalized linear mixed models (GLMM).
6. Application of the methodology to deep learning models, demonstrating the practicality of the approach.
7. Comprehensive numerical experiments on simulated and real data to validate the methodology.
8. A discussion of the implications and potential extensions of the methodology.
1.4
The paper's structure

the bias-corrected CV estimator for general models and prediction criteria. In Section 3, we

cluster structure and the spatial GRF structure. In Section 4, we describe the parametric
bootstrap approach for estimating the bias and provide details on the efficient approximations.
In Section 5, we test our methodology on various simulated and real data examples. In Section
6, we discuss the implications of our findings and potential extensions. The proofs of the key
results are deferred to the appendices, where we also provide additional technical details.
